title: Active and Passive Voice
storyTitle: Two Camera Angles in the Royal Courtroom

steps.settingDescription: Witnesses are describing how the courtyard bell went missing. Maharaj Vakya wants two camera angles on the same fact: who did it vs. what happened to the bell!

dialogues.line: Angle One: 'The carpenter repaired the golden bell.' Now flip the spotlight onto the bell itself—without losing a single drop of tense!
Easy! 'The golden bell repaired by the carpenter!' And for 'The bell fell down', it's 'The bell was fallen down'!
Two huge traps, Chikoo! First, you forgot the passive auxiliary 'was' ('was repaired')! Second, 'fell' is INTRANSITIVE—it has no object, so it can NEVER become passive!
Passive Voice ALWAYS follows one golden core: [BE matched to original tense] + [Past Participle V3]. And smart writers know when to KEEP 'by + agent'—and when to DROP it!

steps.storyCallout: Goal: Transform transitive active sentences into accurate passive forms across tenses and sentence patterns, and decide when to omit 'by + agent'.

steps.stepTitle: Discover: The Passive Engine & Tense Conversion
steps.subtopicTitle: Transitivity Rule, [Be + V3] Formula & Tense Mapping
steps.memoryAidLabel: Memory Aid (Peculiar Definition — Not a Formal Rule)
steps.peculiarDefinition: Active vs. Passive is a camera switch! Active points at the DOER ('Riya painted the wall'); Passive points at the RECEIVER ('The wall was painted by Riya'). To build ANY passive, swap Object → Subject, insert a form of 'BE' dressed in the original tense, and lock the main verb into V3!
steps.formalDefinition: Voice indicates whether the subject performs the action (Active) or receives/undergoes the action (Passive). Only transitive verbs taking an object can passivise. The passive verb group always uses an inflected form of 'be' (expressing the original tense/aspect/modality) followed by the past participle (V3) of the main verb.
steps.simpleExplanation:
Check every tense transformation carefully:
1) Simple Present ('writes') → 'am/is/are + V3' ('is written')
2) Simple Past ('wrote') → 'was/were + V3' ('was written')
3) Present/Past Continuous ('is/was writing') → 'is/was + BEING + V3' ('is being written'—never drop 'being'!)
4) Present/Past Perfect ('has/have/had written') → 'has/have/had + BEEN + V3'
5) Modals / Future ('will/can/must write') → 'modal + BE + V3'
CRITICAL RULE: Intransitive verbs ('sleep, arrive, happen, seem, occur, die, fall') take NO object, so they CANNOT form passives (*was happened, *was arrived are impossible!).

structurePatterns.sample: writes → is written | wrote → was written | is writing → is being written | has written → has been written

structurePatterns.formula: Modal + BE + V3 | Modal + HAVE BEEN + V3 | am/is/are going to + BE + V3
structurePatterns.sample: We must protect forests → Forests must be protected.

realLifeExamples.sentence: The masons are repairing the clock tower right now. → The clock tower is being repaired right now.
realLifeExamples.contextNote: Present Continuous active keeps '-ing' inside passive 'is BEING repaired'.

realLifeExamples.sentence: Someone has stolen my bicycle. → My bicycle has been stolen.
realLifeExamples.contextNote: Omit vague 'by someone'—the receiver ('My bicycle') is the real focus.

correctVsIncorrect.incorrectSentence: The bridge is repairing this week, and an accident was happened yesterday.
correctVsIncorrect.correctSentence: The bridge is being repaired this week, and an accident happened yesterday.
correctVsIncorrect.whyItHappens: Bridges cannot repair themselves (needs passive 'is being repaired'), and intransitive 'happen' can NEVER take passive 'was happened'.

exceptions: Note two-word verbs in the passive: never drop the preposition! 'Everyone laughed at the clown' → 'The clown was laughed AT by everyone.'

steps.storyPrompt: Detective Ira tests two witness reports: "The clerks are checking the royal seals right now."
steps.questionPrompt: Which passive transformation preserves the exact Present Continuous tense?
options: The royal seals are checked right now by the clerks.
The royal seals are being checked right now by the clerks.
The royal seals have been checked right now by the clerks.
The royal seals were being checked right now by the clerks.
acceptedAnswers: The royal seals are being checked right now by the clerks.
steps.hint: Active has 'are checking' (Present Continuous) → plural 'seals' takes 'are' + 'being' + V3 ('checked')!
steps.feedbackCorrect: Detective Ira: "Exact camera angle! 'Are being checked' preserves continuous aspect and plural agreement with 'royal seals'."
steps.feedbackWrongDefault: Keep Present Continuous ('are + -ing') by using 'are being + V3'.

feedbackWrongByOption.The royal seals are checked right now by: Drops 'being', turning Present Continuous into Simple Present habit!
feedbackWrongByOption.The royal seals have been checked right: Shifts aspect to Present Perfect (already completed).

steps.simplerExample: She is painting a poster → A poster is being painted by her.

steps.stepTitle: Checkpoint 2: Fill the Passive Verb Group
steps.storyPrompt: Acharya Vidyadhar transforms: "Before dusk, the volunteers had planted fifty bamboo saplings." → "Before dusk, fifty bamboo saplings ____ planted by the volunteers."
steps.questionPrompt: Type the two missing auxiliary words ('____ ____'):
steps.sentenceTemplate: Before dusk, fifty bamboo saplings ________ planted by the volunteers.
steps.hint: Active has Past Perfect 'had planted' → Past Perfect Passive uses 'had' + 'been' + V3!
steps.feedbackCorrect: Acharya Vidyadhar: "Spot on! Past Perfect Active ('had planted') becomes Past Perfect Passive ('had been planted')."
steps.feedbackWrongDefault: Use 'had been' (Past Perfect passive auxiliary pair) before 'planted'.
steps.simplerExample: She had locked the gate → The gate had been locked by her.

steps.stepTitle: Discover: Special Patterns & When to Omit 'By + Agent'
steps.subtopicTitle: Questions, Imperatives, Two Objects & Agent Omission
steps.memoryAidLabel: Memory Aid (Peculiar Definition — Not a Formal Rule)
steps.peculiarDefinition: Keep 'by + agent' ONLY when the doer is important news ('The telescope was invented by Galileo'). Drop 'by + agent' when the doer is vague ('someone'), obvious ('the police arrested the thief'), or unimportant ('Rice is grown in Assam')!
steps.formalDefinition: Passive voice applies across ditransitive clauses (promoting either indirect or direct object), interrogatives (retaining question inversion and converting 'Who' to 'By whom' / 'Who... by'), imperatives ('Let + object + be + V3' or 'You are advised/requested to...'), and prepositional verbs. Natural style omits 'by + agent' whenever the agent is unknown, generic, or self-evident.
steps.simpleExplanation:
Master these four high-scoring passive patterns:
1) Omitting 'by + agent': Omit 'by someone / by people / by them / by the police' unless needed for meaning ('English is spoken worldwide'—NOT *by people; 'The thief was arrested'—obviously by police!).
2) Two Objects (SVOO): 'Grandmother told us a story' has TWO passives—promoting the person ('We were told a story by Grandmother') is usually most natural, or 'A story was told to us by Grandmother'.
3) Questions & Imperatives: 'Who painted this?' → 'By whom was this painted?' (or 'Who was this painted by?'). Imperative 'Close the door' → 'Let the door be closed' or 'You are requested to close the door' (when 'Please' appears!).
4) Non-'by' Passives & Prepositional Verbs: Some verbs take fixed prepositions instead of 'by' in the passive ('known TO', 'surprised AT', 'pleased WITH', 'filled WITH', 'contained IN'), and phrasal/prepositional verbs MUST keep their particle/preposition ('The doctor was sent FOR'; 'His proposal was laughed AT').

structurePatterns.formula: Who V2 + Obj? → By whom was/were + Obj + V3? | Please + V1 → You are requested to + V1
structurePatterns.sample: Who broke the slate? → By whom was the slate broken? / Please sit down → You are requested to sit down.

structurePatterns.formula: known TO | surprised AT | interested IN | satisfied WITH | filled WITH
structurePatterns.sample: His honesty is known to everyone (NOT *by everyone). / The jar is filled with honey.

realLifeExamples.sentence: Two new bridges have been built across the river this year.
realLifeExamples.contextNote: Omit 'by workers'—the focus is the bridges, and the agent is obvious.

realLifeExamples.sentence: We were deeply impressed by—or rather satisfied with—the teamwork, and our coach is known to every school.
realLifeExamples.contextNote: 'Satisfied with' and 'known to' use fixed non-'by' prepositions.

correctVsIncorrect.incorrectSentence: The elderly woman was well looked by her neighbours, and his kindness is known by all.
correctVsIncorrect.correctSentence: The elderly woman was well looked after by her neighbours, and his kindness is known to all.
correctVsIncorrect.whyItHappens: Never drop 'after' from phrasal verb 'look after' in passive voice, and 'known' takes preposition 'to' (not 'by').

exceptions: Active verbs 'make, see, hear' drop 'to' ('He made me wait'), yet in the PASSIVE they restore 'to' ('I was made to wait').

steps.storyPrompt: Vaani challenges you to turn an active courtroom question into clean passive voice: "Did anyone look after the injured bird?"
steps.questionPrompt: Pick the grammatically accurate passive question:
options: Was the injured bird looked by anyone?
Was the injured bird looked after?
Did the injured bird be looked after?
Were the injured bird looked after?
acceptedAnswers: Was the injured bird looked after?
steps.hint: Keep 'after' attached to 'looked' ('looked after'), start with 'Was' (past singular for 'the injured bird'), and drop vague 'by anyone'!
steps.feedbackCorrect: Vaani: "Spotless! 'Was the injured bird looked after?' keeps the preposition 'after', matches singular 'bird', and drops vague 'by anyone'."

feedbackWrongByOption.Was the injured bird looked by anyone?: Never drop the particle 'after' from 'look after'!

steps.simplerExample: Did they send for the doctor? → Was the doctor sent for?

steps.storyPrompt: Maharaj Vakya asks you to transform "Who wrote this brilliant poem?" into formal passive voice.
steps.questionPrompt: Tap the tiles in order to form the passive question:
acceptedAnswers: By whom was this brilliant poem written?
steps.hint: Start with 'By whom', then 'was', then the full Noun Phrase ('this brilliant poem'), and end with V3 ('written?').
steps.feedbackCorrect: Maharaj Vakya: "Courtroom perfection! 'By whom' + 'was' + Subject + V3!"
steps.feedbackWrongDefault: Order: By whom → was → this brilliant poem → written?
steps.simplerExample: By whom was the bell rung?

steps.settingDescription: With active actors and passive spotlights switching seamlessly without dropping a tense or preposition, Maharaj Vakya closes the hearing.

dialogues.line: Now our court scribes know BOTH when to spotlight the doer ('The carpenter repaired the bell') and when to spotlight the action ('The bell has been repaired'—no vague *by someone!).
Review the tense conversion chart and non-'by' passives in your Grammar Notebook, then complete the 15-question assessment.

summaryRules.heading: Core Passive Formula & Transitivity
summaryRules.ruleSummary: Only transitive verbs (with objects) can become passive. Match 'be' to the active verb's tense/aspect and follow with Past Participle V3.
summaryRules.formulaOrPattern: Simple: is/was + V3 | Continuous: is/was BEING + V3 | Perfect: has/had BEEN + V3 | Modal: modal + BE + V3
summaryRules.example: They are cleaning the hall → The hall is being cleaned.

summaryRules.heading: When to Keep vs. Omit 'By + Agent'
summaryRules.ruleSummary: Omit 'by + agent' when the doer is unknown ('someone'), generic ('people, we'), or obvious ('the police'). Keep 'by + agent' when naming the specific doer adds vital information.
summaryRules.formulaOrPattern: Tea is grown in Assam (agent omitted) vs. Gitanjali was written by Tagore (agent kept).
summaryRules.example: Two laptops were stolen from the lab last night.

summaryRules.heading: Questions, Imperatives & Non-'By' Passives
summaryRules.ruleSummary: 'Who...?' becomes 'By whom + aux + S + V3?'. Keep phrasal particles/prepositions ('laughed at'). Use fixed prepositions after stative passives ('known to', 'filled with', 'surprised at').
summaryRules.formulaOrPattern: Please help him → You are requested to help him | Let + Obj + be + V3
summaryRules.example: Her courage is known to everyone; the child was well looked after.

memoryAids: Camera Switch: Active focuses on DOER; Passive focuses on RECEIVER—never drop 'BEING' in continuous or 'BEEN' in perfect!
Intransitive Stop Sign: verbs with NO object (happen, arrive, sleep, die, fall) can NEVER go passive (*was happened is impossible!).

commonMistakes.incorrectSentence: The bridge is repairing right now, and a storm was occurred last night.
commonMistakes.correctSentence: The bridge is being repaired right now, and a storm occurred last night.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Continuous passive needs 'is being repaired', and intransitive 'occur' cannot take passive voice.

commonMistakes.incorrectSentence: His kindness is known by all, and the prisoner was made wait.
commonMistakes.correctSentence: His kindness is known to all, and the witness was made to wait.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: 'Known' pairs with 'to' (not 'by'), and passive 'was made' restores 'to' before the infinitive.

exceptions: Imperative passives use 'Let + object + be + V3' ('Let the lamp be lit') or 'You are requested/ordered/advised to...' (especially for requests with 'please' or intransitive commands like 'Stand up').
textbookNotes: Consolidated across Assam Ch. 11 (Voice), Punjab IX Ch. 6 (Voice), and Odisha X Ch. 9 (The Passive).

questions.questionText: Change into Passive Voice: "The village artisans wove these bamboo baskets."
options: These bamboo baskets are woven by the village artisans.
These bamboo baskets were woven by the village artisans.
These bamboo baskets were weaving by the village artisans.
These bamboo baskets had been woven by the village artisans.
questions.explanation: Active verb 'wove' is Simple Past → plural subject 'These bamboo baskets' takes 'were' + V3 'woven'.
distractorRationales: Correct: Simple Past plural passive 'were woven'.

questions.questionText: Change into Passive Voice: "The gardeners were watering the saplings at dawn."
options: The saplings were watered by the gardeners at dawn.
The saplings were being watered by the gardeners at dawn.
The saplings are being watered by the gardeners at dawn.
The saplings had been watered by the gardeners at dawn.
questions.explanation: Past Continuous ('were watering') preserves progressive aspect with 'were being + V3' ('were being watered').
distractorRationales: Omits 'being', changing aspect to Simple Past.
Correct: Past Continuous passive 'were being watered'.
questions.grammarRule: Past Continuous Active (was/were + V-ing) → Passive (was/were + being + V3).

questions.questionText: Which sentence CANNOT be converted into Passive Voice because its verb is intransitive?
options: The librarian arranged the encyclopaedias.
A sudden rainbow appeared above the hills.
Someone delivered two telegrams.
The chef baked warm saffron buns.
questions.explanation: 'Appeared' has no direct object ('above the hills' is a place phrase), so it is intransitive and cannot become passive (*was appeared is impossible).
questions.grammarRule: Only transitive verbs with objects can be turned into the passive voice.

questions.questionText: Which passive transformation sounds MOST natural for: "Someone has swept the courtyard cleanly"?
options: The courtyard has been swept cleanly by someone.
The courtyard has been swept cleanly.
The courtyard is swept cleanly by someone.
The courtyard was being swept cleanly.
questions.explanation: Drop indefinite agents like 'by someone' or 'by people' in natural passive sentences while preserving Present Perfect ('has been swept').
distractorRationales: Correct: Present Perfect passive with vague agent omitted.
questions.grammarRule: Omit 'by someone / by people / by them' when the agent is unknown or unimportant.

questions.questionText: Convert into Passive Voice: "Every citizen must obey traffic signals."
options: Traffic signals must obeyed by every citizen.
Traffic signals must be obeyed by every citizen.
Traffic signals are must obeyed by every citizen.
Traffic signals must have obeyed by every citizen.
questions.explanation: Modals form the passive with 'modal + be + V3' ('must be obeyed').
distractorRationales: Missing 'been' and shifts to past deduction.
questions.grammarRule: Modal Active (modal + V1) → Modal Passive (modal + be + V3).

questions.questionText: Change into formal Passive Voice: "Please return library books within seven days."
options: Let library books be please returned within seven days.
You are requested to return library books within seven days.
Library books are requested to return within seven days.
You were ordered to return library books within seven days.
questions.explanation: Polite imperative requests beginning with 'Please' convert naturally to 'You are requested to + V1'.
distractorRationales: Books cannot be requested to act.
questions.grammarRule: Convert polite 'Please + V1' imperatives into 'You are requested to + V1'.

questions.questionText: Choose the accurate passive preposition: "Her disciplined voice is known ____ everyone, and we were surprised ____ the sudden outcome."
options: by / by
to / at
with / to
for / in
questions.explanation: In standard secondary grammar, 'known' takes 'to' ('known to everyone') and 'surprised/astonished/amazed' take 'at' ('surprised at').
questions.grammarRule: Use idiomatic prepositions in stative passives: known TO, surprised AT, interested IN, filled WITH.

questions.questionText: Which TWO passives are BOTH valid conversions of "The principal awarded Meera a scholarship"?
options: 'Meera was awarded a scholarship by the principal' and 'A scholarship was awarded to Meera by the principal'
'A scholarship awarded Meera' and 'Meera awarded a scholarship'
'The principal was awarded Meera' and 'Meera was awarded by scholarship'
'Meera has been awarded' and 'A scholarship is awarded'
questions.explanation: In SVOO, either the Indirect Object ('Meera') or Direct Object ('A scholarship') can become the passive subject.
distractorRationales: Correct: both person-subject and thing-subject passives preserve meaning and tense.
Changes Simple Past tense to Present Perfect/Present.
questions.grammarRule: Ditransitive (SVOO) clauses allow two passives by promoting either the Indirect or Direct Object.

questions.questionText: Turn into Passive Voice: "Nobody laughed at the beginner's accent."
options: The beginner's accent was not laughed.
The beginner's accent was not laughed at.
The beginner's accent did not laughed at.
The beginner's accent wasn't laughing at.
questions.explanation: Keep the verb's preposition ('at') attached after V3 ('was not laughed at'), and reflect 'Nobody' via negative 'was not'.
questions.grammarRule: Never drop particles or prepositions belonging to phrasal/prepositional verbs in the passive.

questions.questionText: Convert into Passive Voice: "The engineers will have tested the turbine before Friday."
options: The turbine will be tested before Friday by the engineers.
The turbine will have been tested by the engineers before Friday.
The turbine will have being tested by the engineers before Friday.
The turbine would have been tested by the engineers before Friday.
questions.explanation: Future Perfect ('will have tested') converts to 'will have been + V3' ('will have been tested').
distractorRationales: Correct: Future Perfect passive 'will have been tested'.
questions.grammarRule: Future Perfect Active (will have + V3) → Passive (will have been + V3).

questions.questionText: Convert back into natural ACTIVE Voice: "Three solar panels were installed on the school roof yesterday."
options: The school roof installed three solar panels yesterday.
Technicians (or Someone) installed three solar panels on the school roof yesterday.
Three solar panels have installed technicians yesterday.
Technicians were installed three solar panels yesterday.
questions.explanation: When reversing an agentless passive ('were installed') back to Active Voice, supply a logical agent ('Technicians' / 'Workers' / 'Someone') as the Subject with Simple Past 'installed'.
distractorRationales: Correct: supplies logical subject + Simple Past active verb.
questions.grammarRule: When changing an agentless passive to active, supply an appropriate subject (e.g., someone, workers, people) matching the verb tense.

questions.questionText: Passivise the infinitive cleanly: "There is no time to lose."
options: There is no time to be losing.
There is no time to be lost.
No time is being lost there.
There is no time lost.
questions.explanation: 'There is + Noun + to + V1' converts into 'There is + Noun + to be + V3' ('There is no time to be lost').
distractorRationales: Continuous passive infinitive is unidiomatic here.
questions.grammarRule: Passive infinitives follow the pattern 'to be + V3' ('work to be done', 'rules to be followed').

questions.questionText: Convert into Passive Voice: "The captain made the lazy sentry march twice around the yard."
options: The lazy sentry was made march twice around the yard by the captain.
The lazy sentry was made to march twice around the yard by the captain.
The lazy sentry made to march twice around the yard.
The lazy sentry was making to march twice around the yard.
questions.explanation: Although active 'made + object' uses bare 'march', passive 'was made' requires the 'to'-infinitive: 'was made to march'.
distractorRationales: Active 'was making' instead of passive 'was made'.
questions.grammarRule: Active 'make + obj + V1' becomes Passive 'be made + to + V1'.

questions.questionText: In scientific lab reports and formal notices (e.g., "Copper is heated in a test tube"), why is Passive Voice preferred?
options: Because the process or result matters more than naming who held the test tube
Because active voice is always ungrammatical in science
Because passive voice has no verbs
Because passive sentences cannot use past tense
questions.explanation: Passive voice keeps scientific writing objective by spotlighting the material and process rather than repeating 'I' or 'we'.
distractorRationales: Active voice is grammatical, just more personal.
Passive sentences have full verb groups.
Passive works across past, present, and future.
questions.grammarRule: Choose passive voice when the receiver, process, or result is more important than the doer.

questions.storyContext: Maharaj Vakya checks the final courtroom record.
questions.questionText: Convert into Passive Voice: "Have the scouts pitched the blue tent?"
options: Has the blue tent been pitched by the scouts?
Have the blue tent been pitched by the scouts?
Was the blue tent pitched by the scouts?
Is the blue tent being pitched by the scouts?
questions.explanation: Plural active 'Have the scouts' flips to singular passive subject 'the blue tent', so auxiliary 'Have' must change to 'Has' ('Has the blue tent been pitched...?').
distractorRationales: Changes Present Perfect to Simple Past.
Changes Present Perfect to Present Continuous.
questions.grammarRule: Always adjust the passive auxiliary ('is/are', 'has/have', 'was/were') to match the NEW passive subject.
